title: Matroid Secretary Conjecture
short_statement: Random-order selection under a matroid constraint now has a general constant-factor result, followed by a sharp e-competitive preprint.
open_problem: The original constant-competitive target is answered affirmatively by Singla's Theorem 3.1; the later combined preprint reports the sharp ratio e. This entry is retained as a reported resolution, not an invitation to solve an unaddressed conjecture.
background: A single-choice secretary rule must balance learning a threshold against losing valuable early arrivals. Matroids replace the single choice by an independence constraint, so accepting an element can block several later choices. General guarantees progressed from logarithmic to doubly logarithmic dependence on rank before the 2026 papers. The distinction between adversarial weights in random order and independently sampled values is essential: prophet inequalities alone did not settle this secretary question.
full_statement: Let $M=(E,\mathcal{I})$ be a matroid on ground set $E$ with independent sets $\mathcal{I}$, equipped with weights $w:E\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ assigned by an adversary. The elements of $E$ are presented to an online algorithm one at a time in uniformly random order; the algorithm knows the matroid (via an independence oracle) but not the weights in advance. Upon each arrival, the algorithm observes the element's weight and must irrevocably accept or reject it, subject to the constraint that the set of accepted elements always remains in $\mathcal{I}$. Let $\mathrm{OPT}$ denote a maximum-weight independent set of $M$ and $\mathrm{ALG}$ the accepted set. The Matroid Secretary Conjecture asks: does there exist a universal constant $c$ (independent of the matroid and weights) and an online algorithm such that $\mathbb{E}[w(\mathrm{ALG})]\ge \frac{1}{c}\,w(\mathrm{OPT})$ for every matroid $M$ and every weighting $w$? The strong form posits that $c=e$ is achievable. This historical conjecture is reported solved by the 2026 theorem in the What Is Known section; the present task is verification of that claim.
known_results:
Sahil Singla, 'The Matroid Secretary Conjecture is True' (arXiv:2609.14555v2, September 29, 2026), Theorem 3.1, gives each element of the canonical optimum acceptance probability at least $1/4$. Summing weighted indicators gives expected value at least $\mathrm{OPT}/4$, settling the original constant-factor target in the stated model. Only $n$ is known upfront; oracle queries use arrived elements.

The combined preprint by Hamed Abdi, Kiarash Banihashem, MohammadTaghi Hajiaghayi, Zhiyi Huang, Danny Mittal, and Sahil Singla (arXiv:2611.08869v1), Theorem 6.1, strengthens this to optimal ratio $e$. Its expected polynomial implementation is in an augmented real-RAM model with exact logarithms, exponentials, and uniform real draws; it is not a polynomial bit-complexity theorem. The rank-one lower bound makes the competitive ratio sharp. These preprints address the historical question; this repository has not independently certified their proofs.

progress.summary: Singla's September theorem resolves the original target; the November combined preprint reports the sharp constant. The theorem, online simulation, snapshot argument, and subsequent computational model were checked, not the entire proof chain.

counterexample_rationale: Search is now relevant to checking a claimed algorithm or proof, not to treating the historical conjecture as unaddressed.
alphaevolve_rationale: Finite-instance checks can test implementations and proof invariants, but cannot certify a universal competitive guarantee.

literature.synthesis: The 4-competitive result already answers the original question. The combined paper merges prior contributions and improves the ratio, so these should not be counted as independent proofs of the sharp theorem. See What Is Known for the computational-model qualification.

reviewed.ref: Babaioff, Immorlica, Kleinberg, 'Matroids, Secretary Problems, and Online Mechanisms', SODA 2007
reviewed.result: Introduces the matroid secretary problem, gives an $O(\log k)$-competitive algorithm for general matroids ($k$ = rank) and constants for graphic, truncated partition, and bounded-degree transversal matroids; explicitly poses the constant-competitiveness open question.

reviewed.ref: Lachish, 'O(log log Rank) Competitive-Ratio for the Matroid Secretary Problem', FOCS 2014
reviewed.result: Historical $O(\log\log\operatorname{rank})$ guarantee; superseded by the 2026 claim.

reviewed.ref: Feldman, Svensson, Zenklusen, 'A Simple O(log log(rank))-Competitive Algorithm for the Matroid Secretary Problem', SODA 2015 / Math. OR 2018
reviewed.result: Independent, much simpler and order-oblivious $O(\log\log\operatorname{rank})$-competitive algorithm with vastly better constants.

reviewed.ref: Bahrani, Beyhaghi, Singla, Weinberg, 'Formal Barriers to Simple Algorithms for the Matroid Secretary Problem', WINE 2022
reviewed.result: Impossibility results showing that natural classes of greedy algorithms and randomized partition algorithms — which contain the algorithms resolving known special cases — cannot resolve the matroid secretary conjecture.

reviewed.ref: Bérczi, Livanos, Soto, Verdugo, 'Matroid Secretary via Labeling Schemes', IPCO 2025 (arXiv 2411.12069)
reviewed.result: General framework analyzing greedy-like MSP algorithms via matroid languages and Poisson point processes; settles laminar greedy-improving probability-competitiveness at exactly $1-\ln 2\approx 0.3068$ and gives $0.2693$ (simple graphs) / $0.2504$ (general graphs) for graphic matroids.

reviewed.ref: Banihashem, Hajiaghayi, Kowalski, Krysta, Mittal, Olkowski, 'Beating Competitive Ratio 4 for Graphic Matroid Secretary', ESA 2025 (arXiv 2501.08846)
reviewed.result: First improvement below the ratio-4 barrier for graphic matroids: 3.95-competitive in general and 3.77 for simple graphs; also shows no algorithm beats $e$ even on graphs of girth $\ge g$ for any constant $g$.

reviewed.ref: Hamed Abdi, Kiarash Banihashem, MohammadTaghi Hajiaghayi, Zhiyi Huang, Danny Mittal, Sahil Singla, 'As Easy as Rank One: Optimal Algorithms for Matroid Secretary and Single-Sample Matroid Prophet' (2026)
reviewed.result: Theorems 1.1 and 6.1 address this conjecture; see the What Is Known section.

reviewed.ref: Sahil Singla, The Matroid Secretary Conjecture is True (2026), arXiv:2609.14555v2
reviewed.result: Theorem 3.1 addresses the original constant-factor target; see What Is Known. Sections 2-3 explain feasibility and the online reduction.

agent_guidance.suitable_approaches: Audit the new theorem's online information restrictions, exchange arguments, and reduction to expected weight.
agent_guidance.verification_notes: Check all matroids and weight assignments, uniformly random arrival order, feasibility, oracle access, and the asserted sharp constant. Finite simulations are not proof. Separate competitive-ratio existence, expected real-arithmetic complexity, and binary-input bit complexity; the combined paper explicitly distinguishes them.
